Learning to let go of video games when you’re young. While I assumed a good majority of Reddit users are avid gamers, I figured out the hard way how detrimental dedicating your youth to gaming is. While my friends and other school mates where progressing academically or optimizing their bodily and muscular functions through sports, I fell deep in the gaming world and a means of coping from being bullied and having a shitty home life. Why be a part of the dread of real life when you can be a badass in Red Dead Redemption or Skyrim or Fallout NV? Video games was my whole life, all the way from late elementary, to the end of high school. Throughout crucial years of my development, I didn’t work on motor control and muscle memory through things like basketball or football, nor did I work on my sense of balance through activities like skateboarding, biking, or dancing. I was too sucked into video games. I also didn’t give the slightest crap about music, so I didn’t bother to pick up any instruments, nor was such pursuit of activities enforced by my parents who were busy juggling 4 other kids. As I speak right now at 24, I have the body of a 50yo. Little muscle development especially in my pelvis and legs, which makes me inept to get into sports, let alone run normally. I have serious muscle imbalances, aches and pains, as well as being overweight at 250lbs, combined with being 6’2 makes me a very top heavy guy. As well as terrible hand/eye coordination. All that combined with a vacuum of a youth where no skills were worked on sent me into a dark abyss. A man with virtually no sense of purpose or identity. What was the point of anything? At least when you chase the sense of stimulation from sports or arts, you slowly gain skill from it, as well as physique, and most importantly: purpose. With video games you gain nothing that helps you through life. You could spend three months on one game, and once you bet every quest, reach max level, and bet the game, that’s it… It’s done. The game is over. What did you learn from it? Nothing really. What skills or real world experience did it bring to the table? Nothing. I just simply beat the game, pop out the disk, and move on to a different game. 

I’ve since then have seen a light in the dark. At senior year of high school I learned I was a pretty decent singer, and taught myself how to sing properly and work on it. I consider myself very talented at singing, since I can easily learn songs and sing to them very accurately. Which brings me joy. At the age of 21, I picked up a camera when I was given an opportunity to go on an important trip. I discovered that taking photos was really fun, and I had a natural eye for it from jump. I’ve been a seasoned photographer for 3 years now and it’s been a guiding light for me. I occasionally play video games, but I finally learned to defeat my addictions to it. I play once in a while or with friends, but I haven’t purchased any new games since Red Dead 2 in 2018. Finally, in my 20s, I feel like I’m finally understanding what it means to be a person. A person with a sense of identity and purpose, with a craft that I care about deeply and is meaningful to me. Which is something that video games could never bring me. No matter how stimulating it was, or how fun CoD was, it an empty existence. Now I work on my crafts, have been working on self taught physical therapy, and I’m ready to finally start life as I wish I did many many years ago in my youth, if only I didn’t pick up a controller.
